title: Cholesterol treatment and changes in guidelines in an academic medical practice.
text_summary: 本研究旨在探讨美国圣路易斯大学医学院家庭与内科医学医师在胆固醇治疗方面的现状，以及2001年成人治疗小组III（ATPIII）指南与2013年美国心脏病学会/美国心脏协会（ACC/AHA）指南变化对实际处方行为和患者治疗资格的影响。研究选取了2012年1月1日至2013年7月31日期间40-75岁至少有一次门诊就诊的初级保健患者，共4536名患者纳入分析。结果显示，71%的患者符合ATPIII目标，56%的患者符合ACC/AHA指南，较ATPIII目标降低了15%。在高危患者中，43%的患者达到了低密度脂蛋白目标，46%的患者正在服用他汀类药物。总体而言，32%的患者需要开始服用他汀类药物，12%的患者需要增加剂量，6%的患者可以停止服用他汀类药物。根据ATPIII指南被认为低风险的患者中，271名患者符合ACC/AHA指南的治疗资格，而129名患者由于指南的变化从中等风险降至低风险。结论：ACC/AHA指南扩大了推荐服用他汀类药物的患者数量，尤其是那些以前被认为处于中等风险的患者，并将提高许多高危患者的治疗强度。许多有心血管事件风险的患者并未接受基于指南的治疗。新的胆固醇指南可能使治疗决策更加容易。

Cholesterol Treatment and Changes in Guidelines
in an Academic Medical Practice
Martin W. Schoen, MD, MPH,a Joanne Salas, MPH,b Jeffrey F. Scherrer, PhD,b Fred R. Buckhold, MDa
aDepartment of General Internal Medicine and bDepartment of Family and Community Medicine, Saint Louis University School of Medicine,
St. Louis, Mo.
ABSTRACT
BACKGROUND: National guidelines are intended to inﬂuence physician cholesterol treatment practices, yet
few studies have documented the effect of new guidelines on actual prescribing behaviors and impacts on
patient eligibility for treatment. We describe current cholesterol treatment in an academic practice of Family
and Internal Medicine physicians as well the effect of a change in cholesterol treatment guidelines from
2001 Adult Treatment Panel III (ATPIII) to 2013 American College of Cardiology/American Heart As-
sociation (ACC/AHA) guidelines.
METHODS: Medical records were extracted from primary care patients aged 40-75 years with at least one
outpatient visit from January 1, 2012 to July 31, 2013; patients were included if they had records of
cholesterol testing, blood pressure measurement, sex, race, and smoking status. Patients were classiﬁed into
ATPIII and ACC/AHA categories based on clinical variables (eg, diabetes, hypertension, atherosclerotic
cardiovascular disease), Framingham Risk Score, and 10-year atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease risk.
RESULTS: There were 4536 patients included in the analysis. Of these, 71% met ATPIII goals and 56% met
ACC/AHA guidelines, a 15% decrease. Forty-three percent of high-risk patients met their low-density li-
poprotein goals and 46% were on statins. Overall, 32% of patients would need to be started on a statin, 12%
require an increased dose, and 6% could stop statins. Of patients considered low risk by ATPIII guidelines,
271 would be eligible for treatment by ACC/AHA guidelines, whereas 129 patients were shifted from
intermediate risk to low risk with the change in guidelines.
CONCLUSIONS: The ACC/AHA guidelines expand the number of patients recommended to receive statins,
particularly among patients who were previously thought to be at moderate risk, and would increase the
intensity of treatment for many patients at high risk. Signiﬁcant numbers of patients at risk for cardio-
vascular events were not receiving guideline-based treatment. New cholesterol guidelines may make
treatment decisions easier.

Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of mortality in
the US, leading to almost 600,000 deaths annually.1 On
November 12, 2013, the American College of Cardiology/
American Heart Association (ACC/AHA) guidelines2 for
treatment of cholesterol and atherosclerotic cardiovascular
risk were released, supplanting the Adult Treatment Panel
III (ATPIII) guidelines that were originally published in
20013 and revised in 2004.4 In ATPIII, low-density lipo-
protein (LDL) levels were the target of therapy based on the
correlation between higher levels of LDL cholesterol and
risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, resulting in
various LDL treatment goals of LDL based on atheroscle-

Several criticisms of the guide-
lines stem from the movement
away from the use of LDL targets
and the development and use of the ASCVD risk estimator
that creates the potential to have large numbers of patients
newly classiﬁed as in need of risk reduction utilizing a statin
medication.7 Subsequent validation of the ASCVD risk
estimation from pooled cohort equations in complementary
populations showed moderate to good risk prediction, espe-
cially in patients without diabetes with LDL between 70 and
189 mg/dL, the population in whom there are signiﬁcant
questions about statin initiation.8 Similarly, there may be a
subset of the general population previously on a statin or
other lipid-lowering agent that may no longer (or never did)
require a lipid-lowering medication.
Prior studies have shown that despite changes in treatment
guidelines, not all patients are prescribed indicated therapy,9
and it may take years after a new guideline is published for
providers to improve compliance.10 This may be due in part
to poor patient adherence to statin therapy,11 although
provider factors,12 patient’s race, and follow-up rate impact
prescribing patterns.13 Although estimates can be made
from national health databases,14 data from large medical
record databases captures the real world of treatment-seeking
patients engaged with primary care providers. Using real-
world data also overcomes exclusion criteria and nonre-
sponse, allowing for potentially more accurate measures of
prescribing and a more generalizable sample. The present
study analyzed patient data of a large clinical practice
to provide an assessment of current cholesterol-lowering
therapy prescribing patterns, and how a change in treat-
ment recommendations might affect patient care.
METHODS
SLUCare is the academic clinical practice of the School of
Medicine at Saint Louis University, based in Saint Louis,
Missouri. The Division of General Internal Medicine and
Department of Family Medicine include approximately
115 physicians, resident trainees, and associated staff at
3 ambulatory care clinics that see an average of approxi-
mately 13,000 unique patients per year. A Primary Care
Patient Data registry was created by extracting records from
27,225 patients (Family Medicine ¼ 10,994, General
Internal Medicine ¼ 16,231) who
had at least one encounter (eg,
ofﬁce visit, procedure visit, or
clinical support) between July 1,
2008 and July 31, 2013. The Pri-
mary Care Patient Data registry
contains

history, demographics, laboratory
orders, referrals, and vital signs.
Our institutions’ Institutional Re-
view Board approved the devel-
opment of the registry and subsequent analysis.
All patients aged 40-75 years whose last status was
“alive” with at least one visit from January 1, 2012 to July
31, 2013 were eligible for the study (n ¼ 9808, Figure 1).
Patients were included if biometric variables of sex, race,
blood

in

total cholesterol values, and statin dose were available in the
registry (n ¼ 4535). Clinical atherosclerotic cardiovascular
disease was obtained based on collection of ICD-9 codes for
coronary artery disease, peripheral vascular disease, and
cerebrovascular disease. Patients diagnosed with type II
diabetes and patients with diagnosed hypertension were also
identiﬁed by ICD-9-CM codes.
Patients in the cohort were deﬁned as statin users if there
was a prescription written for a statin from January 1, 2011
through the end of the study period. We included medica-
tions from the year prior because most statins are prescribed
for a year and patients may not require a new prescription at
every visit and may not have repeat visits in the study
period. Dose and type of statin was determined from the last
available statin prescription or from historical prescription
data entered by medical staff, as reported by the patient.
Statin dose intensity was classiﬁed as low, moderate, or high
based on 2013 ACC/AHA guidelines.2 The use of other
lipid-lowering agents was deﬁned as any prescription from
1 year prior (January 1, 2011) to the end of the study time
period. The last available data point was used to deﬁne
biometric and laboratory data (LDL, HDL, total cholesterol,
body mass index, blood pressure, hemoglobin A1c, and
smoking status). Demographic characteristics included age,
sex, and reported race.

patients into various risk strata according to the 2004
updated ATPIII guidelines, and assessed whether they were
at treatment goals, based on target LDL levels. Patients were
then re-classiﬁed into risk strata based on the 2013 ACC/
AHA guidelines, using clinical characteristics and ASCVD
risk estimation. The ATPIII treatment groups were then
cross-tabulated to the ACC/AHA classiﬁcation to identify
patients in the ATPIII group who would have a potential

RESULTS
The number of eligible patients was 4536 (Figure 1), with
an average age of 56.7 years (SD 9.1). Table 1 describes
the demographic characteristics of the study population.
There were more female patients (60%) than male. The
racial distribution of eligible patients was appropriate for
the area of St. Louis that SLUCare serves, with 53%
white (Caucasian), 44% Black (African-American), and
3% other race. Approximately 10% of the cohort had
atherosclerotic vascular disease, and 12% were actively
smoking. Statins were prescribed to 26.5% of the cohort.
Figure 2 displays the number and percentage of patients
receiving treatment and reaching their therapeutic goal
based on risk stratiﬁcation, according to ATPIII guidelines,
with patients with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease
shown with both LDL goal of <100 mg/dL and the optional
goal of <70 mg/dL. Based on the lipid levels available,
over two-thirds (71%) of the patients achieved ATPIII
cholesterol treatment goals. Fifty-four percent of patients with
clinical atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease achieved goal
cholesterol levels of <100 mg/dL, while only 22% reached
the optional goal of LDL <70 mg/dL. There was a trend for
increasing attainment of cholesterol goals as atherosclerotic
cardiovascular disease risk diminished; 99% of patients
reached the minimal cholesterol-lowering goal of LDL <190
mg/dL (P for trend <.001).
Forty-three percent of high-risk patients with athero-
sclerotic cardiovascular disease, diabetes, or FRS >20%
met the LDL goal of <100 mg/dL, and 46% were treated
with statins, with an additional 4% taking nonstatin lipid
medicines. Notably, 17% of the atherosclerotic cardiovas-
cular disease group, 36% of the diabetes and high Fra-
mingham risk group, and 33% of people with 2 risk factors
and 10%-20% Framingham risk score were not at their goal
LDL and were not receiving any treatment for their hyper-
lipidemia. In total, 29% of patients were receiving medi-
cines to treat their cholesterol, and statins were prescribed to
92% of treated patients, with some patients on dual
cholesterol treatment.

DISCUSSION
In our evaluation of real-world cholesterol management in a
large, academic group practice, we found that treatment
would be affected considerably by the ACC/AHA guide-
lines on cholesterol reduction management. The 2013
ACC/AHA guidelines shifted away from an emphasis on
LDL treatment targets as recommended by ATPIII guide-
lines to treatment based on calculated cardiovascular
risk. Across all risk categories, the ACC/AHA treatment
regimens will result in an increased prescribing of statins.
Over 90% of patients with the 3 highest risk categories
(atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, LDL >190 mg/dL,
and diabetes & ASCVD risk 7.5%) will need a modiﬁ-
cation of their statin dosage using the ACC/AHA guidelines.
The majority of these patients were known to be at risk of
cardiovascular events and therefore intensive treatment
would likely be deemed acceptable by practicing clinicians.
ATPIII categories did not differentiate patients with diabetes
into various risk strata. The separation of patients with
diabetes into the moderate and high-risk groups according to
ACC/AHA resulted in the re-categorization of 165 of 799
(21%)
diabetics
without
atherosclerotic
cardiovascular
disease into lower-risk categories. Almost half (47%) of
those patients are currently not on treatment, but would be
eligible for a statin under new guidelines. Additionally, 376
of those patients were at their therapeutic goals according to
the ATPIII, but are not according to ACC/AHA recom-
mendations and would therefore now require a statin. In
contrast, we found that a small number of patients may have
their statin discontinued. Many of these have moderate or
low Framingham risk scores (10-20 or <10) and scored
<7.5% on the ASCVD risk estimator.
The largest potential change in prescribing practices with
the new ACC/AHA guidelines was in the patients who were
not diabetic and did not have clinical atherosclerotic
cardiovascular disease (n ¼ 3213, 71% of entire cohort).
Two-thirds (68%) of this group had an LDL <130 mg/dL
(n ¼ 2182, 48% of all patients). However, 1075 (50.3%)
have >7.5% ASCVD risk, meaning they should be pre-
scribed a moderate- to high-intensity statin. Age appears to
be the driving factor for this elevation of risk, and 72% of
these patients with ASCVD risk 7.5% are 60 years of age
or older. In this group without diabetes or atherosclerotic
cardiovascular disease and with an LDL <130 mg/dL, the
odds of having an ASCVD risk >7.5% if older than
60 years is 15.4 (95% conﬁdence interval 12.4-19.3, data
not shown). Further examination of the ASCVD risk esti-
mator reveals that for patients with optimal risk factors
(total cholesterol 170 mg/dL, HDL of 50 mg/dL, systolic
blood pressure of 110 mm Hg, and without diabetes, hy-
pertension, or smoking), ASCVD risk is 7.5% for white men
at age 63 years and for black men at age 66 years. ASCVD
risk is 7.5% or greater for white women at age 71 years and
black women at age 70 years who have optimal risk factors.
These patients older than 60 years and their providers
previously may have thought their normal or low cholesterol
values were protective for cardiovascular disease. In several
critiques of the new guidelines, this broad use of statins in
moderate-risk populations has garnered the most atten-
tion.7,16 Data before the widespread use of statins, however,

suggest that 62% of cardiovascular deaths occur in patients
with a serum cholesterol level <240 mg/dL,17 suggesting
that many patients may be undertreated given the efﬁcacy of
statin medications in atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease
risk reduction. Thus, the ACC/AHA guidelines, while
tailored to the reduction of risk for the individual patient,
may be addressing primary prevention risk for the US
population as a whole.18-20
Much of the study population was not receiving optimal
treatment. Less than half (46%) of the 3 highest ATPIII risk
groups met their LDL targets and only 45% were on treat-
ment. To some extent, this reﬂects some of the limitations in
the current study, namely that our dataset could not fully
determine speciﬁc reasons why patients were not meeting
cholesterol goals nor were prescribed statins. Some patients
may have previously been prescribed cholesterol-lowering
medications, but these were stopped due to adverse
events, or patients could be receiving medicines from pro-
viders outside our system and not report them during visits.
Additionally, we used ICD-9 codes present in our medical
records system to determine diagnoses of risk. This may
have resulted in misclassiﬁcation of patients and possible
bias of our data. Conversely, we included statin pre-
scriptions from the year before the beginning of our study in
order to collect all active prescriptions, in case the patient
did not require a new prescription during their visit. This
inclusion could have artiﬁcially increased the number of
patients on statins.
Another interpretation of the data would suggest that
achieving stringent LDL targets according to the ATPIII
guidelines was difﬁcult to achieve and some providers
questioned the use of statins for primary prevention21 as
well as the motives of those involved with guideline
development.22 Furthermore, patient adherence to statin
medicines is poor and is worsened by poor follow-up and
provider continuity,23 and frequently they are not restarted
after adverse events, despite evidence that they can be well
tolerated.24
Given the shift in the cholesterol treatment paradigm
from LDL targets to overall atherosclerotic cardiovascular
disease risk, several ﬁndings are notable. First, the number
of patients aged 40-75 years in our sample who are at
increased risk for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease is
very high: 53% of patients would require therapy with
statin medication. Second, an argument can be made that
treating to a targetedeciding to treat, making a target,
titrating medications from repeated cholesterol meas-
urementseis likely very difﬁcult in a population with
limited health literacy. Making a baseline assessment of
risk, and providing a targeted dose of medication irre-
spective of effects on cholesterol levels might make
treatment easier to achieve. Third, the emphasis on statins
and their dose makes quality assessment easier. Instead of
frequent ascertainment of LDL levels, the question of pa-
tient risk and whether they are taking a statin can be
measured more directly. Last, given the large population
we describe that is now eligible for therapy, further study
is needed to determine the cost-effectiveness of imple-
menting such recommendations.
The strength of this study is to provide a snapshot of
cholesterol treatment in a large, academic practice, and to
examine the effect of large policy shift promulgated by the
new ACC/AHA guidelines on the potential treatment of this
population. In general, we found that a large number of
patients who might not have required or received treatment
under the previous ATPIII guidance would be eligible for
initiating or increasing statins. Conversely, a much smaller
portion of patients previously on cholesterol-lowering
medication would no longer need recommended therapy.
This ﬁnding, on the whole, is consistent with previous
analyses.14
In summary, we provide a description of an academic
practice and how changes in cholesterol treatment recom-
mendations affect our practice. We found that cholesterol
targets were not frequently attained using prior ATPIII
guidelines and many patients were not prescribed statins.
More attention to education and implementation of choles-
terol treatment guidelines is warranted and newer 2013
ACC/AHA guidelines might be more feasible, but would
result in treating a larger percentage of our population.
